content: Chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM), also known as chronic otitis media (COM), is a persistent inflammatory condition of the middle ear and mastoid cavity. It is often caused by polymicrobial infections, meaning it involves multiple microorganisms. The condition is characterized by ear discharge (otorrhoea) through a perforated tympanic membrane. The primary symptoms of CSOM include ear discharge and hearing loss. Antibiotics are commonly used to treat CSOM, as they work to either kill or inhibit the growth of the microorganisms responsible for the infection. These antibiotics can be administered either topically (directly into the ear) or systemically (via oral or injectable routes). They may be used alone or in combination with other treatments, such as ear cleaning (aural toileting). The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of topical antibiotics compared to systemic antibiotics in treating individuals with CSOM. A systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane ENT Register, CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ICTRP, to identify relevant published and unpublished randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The search was completed on March 16, 2020. The inclusion criteria for the study required RCTs with a minimum follow-up period of one week. Participants included both adults and children with chronic ear discharge of unknown cause or CSOM, where the discharge had persisted for more than two weeks. The studies compared the use of topical antibiotics to systemic antibiotics, and they were further categorized based on whether the same type of antibiotic or different types of antibiotics were used in the two treatment groups. The studies also considered whether background treatments, such as aural toileting, were provided to both groups. The analysis followed standard Cochrane methodological procedures, and the GRADE system was used to assess the certainty of the evidence for each outcome. The primary outcomes of interest were the resolution of ear discharge (dry ear), health-related quality of life, and ear pain (otalgia) or local irritation. Secondary outcomes included hearing, serious complications, and ototoxicity. Six studies involving 445 participants were included in the analysis. All studies were assessed to have a high risk of bias. Most participants had confirmed CSOM with documented tympanic membrane perforation. None of the studies reported on the resolution of ear discharge after four weeks or on health-related quality of life. 1. Topical versus systemic administration of the same type of antibiotics (quinolones): Four studies involving 325 participants compared topical ciprofloxacin to systemic (oral) ciprofloxacin. Three studies reported on the resolution of ear discharge at one to two weeks, suggesting that topical administration may slightly improve resolution rates (risk ratio [RR] 1.48, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.24 to 1.76; low-certainty evidence). Aural toileting was either not mentioned or limited to the first visit in these studies. Three studies (265 participants) reported no suspected ototoxicity, but the methods used to assess this were unclear (very low-certainty evidence). None of the studies reported outcomes related to ear pain, serious complications, or hearing, despite hearing being measured in three studies. 2. Topical versus systemic administration of different types of antibiotics (quinolones versus aminoglycosides): One study involving 60 participants compared topical ciprofloxacin to intramuscular gentamicin. Aural toileting was not performed. The resolution of ear discharge at one to two weeks was not measured. The study did not report any adverse effects, leading to the assumption that no ear pain, suspected ototoxicity, or serious complications occurred (very low-certainty evidence). The study stated that no worsening of audiometric function was observed with either local or systemic therapy. 3. Topical versus systemic administration of different types of antibiotics (quinolones versus amoxicillin-clavulanic acid): One study compared topical ofloxacin to oral amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, with all participants receiving suction ear cleaning at the first visit. Due to study limitations and a very small sample size, it is uncertain whether there is a difference between the two groups in resolving ear discharge at one to two weeks (RR 2.93, 95% CI 1.50 to 5.72; very low-certainty evidence). It is also unclear whether there is a difference between the two groups in terms of ear pain, hearing, or suspected ototoxicity (very low-certainty evidence). No outcomes related to serious complications were reported. The authors concluded that there is limited, low-quality evidence available to determine whether topical or systemic antibiotics are more effective in resolving ear discharge in individuals with CSOM. Most of the included studies were conducted over 15 years ago, and the evidence is insufficient to draw definitive conclusions. However, there is some indication that topical antibiotics may be more effective than systemic antibiotics in achieving resolution of ear discharge (dry ear). There is limited evidence comparing different types of antibiotics, and it is unclear whether topical quinolones are superior or inferior to systemic aminoglycosides. These two classes of antibiotics have different adverse effect profiles, but the included studies provided insufficient data to comment on these differences. Overall, adverse effects were poorly reported across the studies.
